extracted.intended_audience: comedians, Fringe performers, festival organisers and general readers interested in the Edinburgh Comedy Awards
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and evaluative criteria governing the Edinburgh Comedy Awards (main prize, Best Newcomer, Panel Prize), including eligibility definitions (e.g., first full-length show = 50 minutes), panel discretion, and noted inclusivity criticisms. Targeted at entrants and those seeking to understand how winners are chosen.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Donald and Eleanor Taffner Best Comedy Show (Main Prize)
rubrics_metrics.description: Awarded 'for the funniest, most outstanding, up-and-coming comic / comedy show / act' at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe. Winner receives a cash prize (stated on page as £10,000). Historically the main prize and formerly known under sponsored names (e.g., Perrier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the headline prize presented to the show judged to be the funniest and most outstanding at the Fringe. Examples/notes on application: in 2017 there were joint winners of the main prize; the prize has recognized a mix of revues and stand-up since a stand-up first won in 1987. The award's name has changed with sponsors; winners are often referred to colloquially as having won 'the Eddie'.

rubrics_metrics.name: DLT Entertainment Best Newcomer Award (Best Newcomer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given to the best 'performer or act who is performing their first full-length show (50 minutes or more)'. Introduced in 1992. The prize amount cited is £5,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newcomers are defined by performing their first full-length show (explicitly 50 minutes or more). While newcomers are eligible for the Best Comedy Show Award, the rules state that no act is allowed to appear on both shortlists in the same year. Example: John Kearns won Best Newcomer (and later Best Comedy Show in consecutive years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel Prize (panel discretion / open eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prize inaugurated in 2006 for which 'all shows are eligible', with the additional feature that 'the award may not be awarded at all, if the panel so choose.' The Panel Prize winner receives a cash prize (noted similarly to Best Newcomer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This prize is discretionary: the judging panel can consider any show at the Fringe and may decide not to give the prize in a given year. Past practice shows flexible outcomes — e.g., in 2008 it was awarded to 'every comedian on the Fringe'; in some years no panel prize was awarded. The Panel Prize can therefore be used to recognise unusual or collective achievements beyond conventional shortlist categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility: show must be at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe
rubrics_metrics.description: The awards are presented to the comedy shows deemed to have been the best at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe in Scotland; thus eligible works are shows performed at that festival.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit operational requirement: to be considered for any of the awards, the show/act must be presented at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe. The page references an external 'Eligibility Rules' source (comedyawards.co.uk) for detailed rules; operational details given on-page include the newcomer definition (first full-length show = 50 minutes or more) and the rule preventing an act appearing on both Best Newcomer and Best Comedy Show shortlists in the same year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusivity and representation considerations (criticisms as evaluative constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: The awards and their shortlists have been criticised for lack of diversity — e.g., years when no female acts were shortlisted (2002), and criticism in 2009 that nominees were all male, all white, English and all performing at the same venue (The Pleasance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not stated as a formal judging criterion on the page, these documented criticisms function as de facto evaluative expectations from commentators and the community: shortlist composition has been scrutinised for gender, racial and venue diversity. Past responses and controversies (including boycotts and alternative awards) indicate public pressure on organisers and judges to consider broader representational factors when selecting nominees and winners.
